title: Beyond and within

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirgun and its twin, sargun: the One beyond every quality and present in every form. Your line was vast and close. What did you look up at, and what small thing did you look at closely? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

Dusk, and in a temple in Guru Nanak's world, priests are lifting trays. On each tray, little lamps, flowers, incense, a pearl or two, waved in circles before an image. It's called aarti, a worship of light. Tradition tells of Guru Nanak watching a ceremony like this, and then stepping outside and singing his own. His tray was much bigger. Guru Nanak's aarti is still sung by Sikhs at the end of the day, and it's a good way into today's idea, because in one hymn it goes as far out as a hymn can go, and then as far in.
screen: `LAMPS ON A TRAY, AT DUSK.` → `GURU NANAK SINGS HIS OWN.` → `AS FAR OUT, THEN AS FAR IN.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens, in paraphrase, like this: the sky is the tray, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls. The breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, and all the forests are flowers. The whole universe is already doing aarti, and no tray in any temple could hold it. That's beyond: the One past every size we can manage. The English word for it is transcendent. Then the same hymn turns, and says, again in paraphrase: in everything there is a light, and that light is You. By that light, everything is lit. Five days ago that line held the many sangats together. Here it sits where Guru Nanak placed it, right after the sky-sized tray, in Sohila, the bedtime prayer. That's within: the One inside every living thing. The English word is immanent. The turn is the point. Guru Nanak doesn't sing two hymns, one for the stars and one for the heart. He sings one. The same One is the sky-sized aarti and the light inside a single person, and you can't keep one and drop the other. Look back at the week. It began by borrowing from one stream, saw many sangats under one Guru, and closed the tour of the streams. Then Sikh thought began: many names, the name Waheguru, nirgun and sargun. Each day circled the same shape. Many streams, one Guru. Many names, one One. Vast and close. This hymn just says it under an open sky. Beyond and within.
screen: `THE SKY IS THE TRAY.` · `IN EVERYTHING, A LIGHT.` · `ONE HYMN, NOT TWO.` · `THE WEEK: MANY, AND ONE.` · then, large: `BEYOND AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up, then inward. If you can, stand at a window or go outside; if not, picture the sky. Settle, and breathe. For the first part of the sit, look up: the sky as a tray, the sun or moon as a lamp, the air moving as incense. Let it be huge. Then close your eyes, and turn the same attention inward, to the warmth of your own breath, the light behind your eyes. Same attention, different direction. The bell holds the time.
Beyond and within. Transcendent and immanent at once: the One past every size, and the light inside every living thing, held in one hymn. Today's word.
Your line: beyond and within. Today, at dusk, look at the sky for one long moment, then at someone near you, and notice the light in both. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sohila at night, which includes Guru Nanak's aarti picturing the sky as the tray of lamps and the light in everything as the One's light; Guru Nanak's aarti is also sung as kirtan in the evening.

original.note: Gurmukhi: light; in the aarti, the light in everything is the One's light.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs believe God is far away above the sky.
what it means: the One is beyond every size and inside every living thing, both at once.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's aarti moves in one hymn from the sky as the tray to the light in everything.
